ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
Consider the following simple model of a bow and arrow. An ideal elastic string has a spring constant $k=10 \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}$ and relaxed length $L=1 \mathrm{~m}$ which is attached to the ends of an inflexible fixed steel rod of the same length $L$ as shown below. A small ball of mass $m=2 \mathrm{~kg}$ and the thread are pulled by its midpoint away from the rod until each individual part of the thread have the same length of the rod, as shown below. What is the speed of the ball in meters per seconds right after it stops accelerating? Assume the whole setup is carried out in zero gravity.

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: On the left side of the figure is a fixed vertical steel rod, labeled with length L. The two ends of the elastic string are respectively connected to the upper and lower ends of the steel rod, and the string is pulled to the right by a small ball at the midpoint, forming a triangle. The upper and lower oblique segments are both labeled L, and the small ball is located on the right side and labeled with mass m. Reasoning: According to the pulled-open state shown in the figure, the length of each segment of the elastic string is L, so the total length of the whole string is 2L. The problem states that the relaxed length of the whole elastic string is L, and the spring constant k=10 N/m, so the initial extension is Δx=2L−L=L. With zero gravity and the steel rod fixed, after release, elastic potential energy is converted into the kinetic energy of the small ball. When the string first returns to the relaxed total length L, the tension is zero and the small ball no longer accelerates. By energy conservation: (1/2)kL^2 = (1/2)mv^2. So v = L√(k/m). Substituting L=1 m, k=10 N/m, m=2 kg: v = √(10/2)=√5≈2.23 m/s.

method.method_draft: First read the diagram as a triangular pulled configuration: a fixed vertical rod on the left has length L, and the elastic string runs from the top rod end to the ball and from the ball to the bottom rod end, with each slanted segment labeled L. Thus, in the pulled state the total string length is 2L. From the text, the string’s relaxed total length is L, spring constant is k=10 N/m, and the ball mass is m=2 kg. Treat the whole string as one ideal spring whose extension is Δx=2L−L=L. In zero gravity and with the rod fixed, conserve mechanical energy: initial elastic energy (1/2)kL^2 becomes the ball’s kinetic energy when the string first reaches its relaxed total length, because then the tension and acceleration vanish. Solve (1/2)m v^2=(1/2)kL^2, giving v=L sqrt(k/m)=sqrt(10/2)=sqrt(5)≈2.23 m/s.

method.method_draft: Read the image as showing the midpoint of the string pulled to the ball, splitting the string into two equal slanted halves, each of current length L, attached to the two ends of a fixed rod of length L. From the text, the original whole string has relaxed length L and spring constant k=10 N/m, so each half has relaxed length L/2. For a uniform ideal elastic string, halving the length doubles the spring constant, so each half has spring constant 2k. In the shown pulled position, each half is stretched from L/2 to L, so each half has extension L/2. The elastic energy stored in one half is (1/2)(2k)(L/2)^2=kL^2/4; for two halves the total is kL^2/2. When the ball reaches the point where the string is relaxed, the tension vanishes and the ball stops accelerating, so this stored energy has become kinetic energy: (1/2)m v^2=kL^2/2. With L=1 and m=2, v=sqrt(kL^2/m)=sqrt(5)≈2.23 m/s.
